strengths: The paper identifies a clear and timely limitation of visual autoregressive generative classifiers: fixed token order imposes a strong inductive bias that can hurt classification. The proposed order-marginalized RandAR classifier is conceptually simple, well motivated, and appropriate for the Algorithms/General contribution type.

Empirical results are strong and broad. RandAR substantially improves over fixed-order AR baselines, prior AR generative classifiers, and diffusion classifiers on ImageNet-Val and multiple OOD benchmarks, with especially convincing gains for RandAR-XL on IN-R, IN-S, and ImageNet-C corruptions.

The efficiency argument is important: even with K-order marginalization, AR likelihood evaluation remains much cheaper than diffusion classifier ELBO estimation, and the paper reports favorable accuracy-runtime tradeoffs on a single A100.

The analysis sections are useful rather than decorative. Per-token likelihood visualizations, token-order ablations, likelihood-estimation ablations, tokenizer/noise augmentation studies, and error analysis help explain why order marginalization improves performance.

The paper compares against a reasonably diverse set of baselines, including discriminative ViTs, DINOv2, diffusion classifiers, joint generative-discriminative models, prior AR classifiers, ResNets, and WILDS robustness baselines. This supports the claim that the method is competitive beyond a narrow benchmark setting.
The manuscript is generally clear and well structured, with equations and figures that make the method easy to understand.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate. The core method is Monte Carlo averaging of log-likelihoods over random token orders using an existing any-order AR model. The paper makes a strong empirical case, but the conceptual step is relatively straightforward once RandAR is available.

Some central evaluations rely on small subsets: 2K subsets are used for IN-Val, IN-S, and ImageNet-C because generative classification over 1000 classes is expensive. This is understandable, but the paper does not report confidence intervals or variance across subset samples, which weakens the strength of fine-grained comparisons.

The theoretical interpretation of the score is somewhat loose. The paper motivates order marginalization via log p(x|c), but the best-performing estimator is the Jensen lower bound E_pi[log p(x|pi,c)], while the direct likelihood estimate performs much worse. This is empirically justified but leaves ambiguity about what probabilistic quantity the classifier is actually optimizing.

Reproducibility is incomplete as written: the abstract says code and models are available but the URL is blank in the provided manuscript. Given the large compute required to pretrain RandAR, DiT, and DINOv2 variants, released checkpoints and exact evaluation subsets are important.

The fairness of some baseline comparisons is not fully airtight. Several models are retrained or evaluated under different training durations, augmentations, tokenizers, and public checkpoints. The authors try to control architecture size and resolution, but remaining differences could materially affect results.

The practical cost remains high despite the relative speedup. Classification requires evaluating all classes across multiple orders, so the method is still expensive for large label spaces compared with discriminative classifiers. The paper acknowledges this but could quantify memory/batching constraints and scaling with class count more explicitly.

WILDS results are promising but limited. The paper reports strong robustness on several datasets, but generative models do not appear to be averaged over multiple random seeds, and some gains over DiT are small or dataset-dependent, especially on FMoW.

strengths: The paper studies a timely and relevant question: whether modern any-order visual autoregressive models can serve as competitive generative classifiers. The focus on token order as an inductive bias is clear and potentially useful for the generative-classification literature.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is fairly thin. The main method is Monte Carlo averaging of RandAR log-likelihoods over random token orders, with a heuristic preference for E[log p(x|pi,c)] over log E[p(x|pi,c)]. This is sensible, but it is largely a repurposing of an existing any-order AR model rather than a substantially new algorithm.

The paper’s strongest claims depend heavily on experimental protocol choices that are not fully convincing. ImageNet-Val, ImageNet-S, and ImageNet-C are evaluated on 2K subsets because of compute cost, but the paper reports no confidence intervals, subset variance, or repeated subsampling. Several reported gains are meaningful, but the limited evaluation weakens the case for broad state-of-the-art claims.

The comparison to diffusion classifiers may be underdeveloped. The paper evaluates DiT/SiT with selected weighting and timestep settings, but diffusion-classifier performance is known to be sensitive to schedules, objectives, noise matching, and implementation details. The claim of consistently outperforming diffusion classifiers would be stronger with more exhaustive tuning, uncertainty estimates, and clearer compute-normalized protocols.

The efficiency claim is not sufficiently transparent. Figure 6 reports seconds per single-image classification on one A100, but the paper does not provide enough detail about batching over classes/orders, implementation optimizations, memory constraints, or wall-clock reproducibility. Since the method still requires evaluating many class/order combinations, practical scalability to larger label spaces remains a concern.

The analysis of why order marginalization helps is suggestive rather than rigorous. Per-token heatmaps and token-accuracy plots are interesting, but the explanations about broader object coverage, prefix lengths, and high-level information are mostly post hoc hypotheses.

The comparison with discriminative and SSL classifiers is somewhat uneven. RandAR remains below DINOv2 in ImageNet accuracy and IN-A, and the paper frames competitiveness strongly while not fully discussing the much higher inference cost and training cost relative to discriminative classifiers.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in places. The abstract says code and models are available but the link is blank in the supplied manuscript, and some baselines are reproduced by the authors without enough reporting of validation, variance, or exact selection criteria to make the comparisons easy to audit.

Overall, the paper has a worthwhile empirical observation and some strong results, but the novelty, rigor of evidence, and transparency of the efficiency/baseline comparisons are not yet convincing enough for acceptance at ECCV.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored question: whether modern visual autoregressive models can serve as strong generative classifiers. The central observation that fixed token order is a limiting inductive bias is well motivated and leads to a simple, effective order-marginalized classifier using any-order AR models.

The empirical evidence is broad and generally convincing. The method improves over fixed-order AR baselines, diffusion classifiers, and prior VAR-based generative classifiers on ImageNet-Val and several ImageNet distribution-shift benchmarks, with especially strong OOD gains. The WILDS experiments further support the robustness claims beyond ImageNet-style shifts.

The analysis sections strengthen the submission: per-token likelihood visualizations, per-token accuracy studies, order/K ablations, likelihood-estimation comparisons, tokenizer/noise-augmentation analysis, and error examples all help explain why order marginalization helps rather than only reporting benchmark numbers.

The efficiency argument is important and practically relevant. Because AR likelihoods can be evaluated in far fewer forward passes than diffusion classifier ELBO estimates, the reported accuracy/latency tradeoff is a meaningful contribution for generative classification.

The paper is clearly written and mostly well organized. It gives enough implementation detail in the appendix to understand the training and evaluation setup, and it makes a useful comparison to strong self-supervised discriminative models rather than only to older supervised baselines.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is relatively modest: the main algorithmic step is Monte Carlo averaging of log-likelihoods over random token orders using an existing any-order AR model. The contribution is valuable empirically, but the conceptual advance is incremental rather than a fundamentally new modeling approach.

The preferred scoring rule is the Jensen lower bound, E[log p(x|pi,c)], rather than the direct order-marginalized likelihood log E[p(x|pi,c)]. This works better empirically, but it weakens the interpretation as exact generative classification under an order-marginalized model; the explanation that it matches the training objective is plausible but not fully theoretically developed.

Several main ImageNet results are reported on 2K subsets for IN-Val, IN-S, and IN-C due to compute. This is understandable, but the paper does not provide confidence intervals, subset sensitivity, or repeated-subset estimates, making it harder to judge the statistical stability of some gaps.

The fairness of some comparisons still has caveats. Different methods use different tokenizers, training recipes, released versus reproduced checkpoints, and in some cases additional augmentations such as latent noise. The authors discuss and ablate some of this, but the strongest conclusions partly depend on many engineering choices.

The efficiency evaluation would benefit from more detail on batching over classes/orders, memory use, hardware utilization, and whether all baselines are optimized similarly. Seconds per image on one A100 is useful, but the reproducibility of the 25x claim is not fully established.

The paper has limited discussion of limitations and societal impact. It notes computational cost and future distillation, but says less about failure modes in high-class-count settings, dependence on the VQ tokenizer, calibration, class priors, or behavior under label imbalance and domain-specific datasets.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored question: whether modern visual autoregressive models can serve as competitive generative classifiers. The focus on token ordering is well motivated and clearly connected to known differences between AR and diffusion generation.

The proposed order-marginalized scoring of any-order AR models is simple, technically plausible, and supported by useful analysis. The per-token likelihood visualizations, per-token accuracy maps, prefix-length study, and K ablations make the central claim more convincing than a pure benchmark paper would.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this area: ImageNet-Val, ImageNet-R/S/A/C, efficiency comparisons, tokenizer ablations, likelihood-estimation ablations, masked-diffusion comparisons, additional AR architecture evidence, ObjectNet/COCO appendix results, and WILDS distribution-shift experiments.

The results are strong. RandAR substantially improves over fixed-order AR baselines and diffusion classifiers, and the comparison to DINOv2 is valuable because it situates generative classification against a much stronger discriminative baseline than is often used.
The efficiency argument is practically important: even with multiple sampled orders, AR scoring is shown to dominate diffusion classifier accuracy-runtime tradeoffs over the tested operating points.
weaknesses: The main methodological novelty is somewhat limited. The work largely repurposes RandAR with Monte Carlo averaging over token orders and uses the training-aligned lower bound as the score. This is a meaningful insight, but it is closer to an effective evaluation/inference strategy than a fundamentally new model or algorithm.

The theoretical framing around estimating p(x|c) is not fully satisfying. The paper states that the true order-marginalized likelihood estimate performs worse and then uses E_pi log p(x|pi,c), mainly justified by training-objective alignment. This is empirically reasonable, but it weakens the interpretation as principled Bayes generative classification and deserves a sharper discussion of calibration and objective mismatch.

Several central ImageNet and corruption results are reported on 2K subsets because of compute. Although the authors state subset-size variation is minor, stronger statistical reporting, confidence intervals, or repeated subset sampling would make the comparisons more convincing, especially for close differences against DINOv2 and across OOD benchmarks.

Baseline fairness is mostly careful but still hard to fully assess. Many baselines are reproduced from scratch, and performance can depend strongly on tokenizer, augmentations, schedules, timestep choices, and weighting. The paper includes useful ablations, but some choices, such as latent noise augmentation for RandAR and selected diffusion evaluation schedules, could still affect the strength of the empirical case.

The method remains computationally expensive for large label spaces: K orders times all classes requires many class-conditioned evaluations, and the reported per-image classification times are still high relative to standard discriminative classifiers. The paper acknowledges this, but the practical deployment story is limited.

The robustness claims are promising but somewhat uneven. RandAR is strong on several OOD settings, but it trails DINOv2 on ImageNet-A and only matches or slightly trails diffusion models in parts of FMoW. The paper sometimes phrases the robustness advantage more broadly than the mixed results warrant.

Reproducibility would benefit from more explicit reporting of compute budgets, random seeds for the large-scale ImageNet experiments, exact evaluated subsets, and a complete code/model URL in the manuscript text.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant question: whether modern autoregressive visual generative models can be competitive generative classifiers. The focus on token ordering is well motivated and provides a clear explanation for why prior fixed-order AR classifiers underperformed.

The proposed order-marginalized scoring method is simple, technically plausible, and well matched to any-order AR models such as RandAR. The empirical finding that averaging over token orders substantially improves classification is convincing within the presented setup.

The experimental coverage is broad: ImageNet validation, several ImageNet distribution-shift benchmarks, WILDS datasets, tokenizer ablations, likelihood-estimation ablations, efficiency comparisons, masked-diffusion connections, and additional baselines.
The results are strong for generative classifiers, especially on OOD benchmarks, and the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff versus standard diffusion classifiers is a meaningful contribution.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with helpful diagnostic visualizations of per-token likelihood contributions and failure cases.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited: the main idea is Monte Carlo averaging of likelihood scores over random token orders using an existing any-order AR model. The paper’s strength is empirical rather than algorithmic, and the claims should be framed accordingly.

The practical relevance remains constrained by the very high cost of generative classification over many classes. Even if faster than diffusion classifiers, the approach is still far slower than discriminative classifiers and requires training large class-conditional generative models.

Some headline comparisons are not fully satisfying. DINOv2 is retrained on ImageNet-1K rather than using the strongest released large-scale model, while several generative baselines are retrained or adapted under different assumptions. This weakens broad claims about matching state-of-the-art SSL or establishing practical superiority.

Several main evaluations use 2K subsets for ImageNet-Val, ImageNet-S, and ImageNet-C due to compute cost. The paper states that larger subsets cause minor variation, but it does not provide confidence intervals or enough statistical detail to assess robustness of close differences.

The theoretical motivation for using the Jensen lower bound as the classifier score is somewhat post hoc. The lower bound may work empirically because it matches the training objective, but it is not the true marginal likelihood and need not preserve class rankings.

The claimed code/model availability is incomplete in the manuscript text, which is a reproducibility concern. The appendix gives many training details, but the computational burden and reliance on reproduced large-scale pretraining still make independent replication difficult.

The limitations discussion is brief and mostly future-work oriented. It should more explicitly discuss compute, energy cost, dependence on labeled class-conditional pretraining, scalability to very large label spaces, and possible failure modes outside image-centric datasets.

strengths: The paper presents a timely and well-motivated re-examination of autoregressive visual generative classifiers. The central observation that fixed token order is a limiting inductive bias for AR-based classification is intuitive, well illustrated, and supported by targeted analysis of order-dependent predictions and per-token likelihood maps.

The proposed order-marginalized classifier is simple, technically sound, and well aligned with any-order AR models. The use of Jensen's lower-bound estimator is justified empirically, and the paper gives a useful connection between any-order AR scoring and masked diffusion objectives.

The empirical evidence is broad and mostly convincing: comparisons cover prior AR classifiers, diffusion classifiers, joint generative-discriminative models, supervised/SSL discriminative baselines, ImageNet variants, selected corruptions, and WILDS-style distribution shifts.

The results are strong for a generative classifier. RandAR substantially improves over fixed-order AR variants and diffusion classifiers, with particularly notable gains on several OOD benchmarks, while retaining a better accuracy/runtime tradeoff than standard diffusion classifier evaluation.

The paper includes helpful ablations on number of order samples, likelihood aggregation strategy, tokenizer choice, latent noise augmentation, AR vs masked-diffusion scoring, model scale, and limited generalization beyond RandAR. These analyses make the main claim more credible.
The writing is generally clear, and the method is easy to reproduce conceptually. The appendix provides many implementation details and baseline settings.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate: the core method is mainly Monte Carlo averaging of order-conditioned log-likelihoods from an existing any-order AR model. The contribution is valuable, but more as an empirical and conceptual reframing than as a substantially new modeling technique.

Some important claims rely on partial evaluations. Several ImageNet results are reported on 2K subsets due to cost, and main-table uncertainty or repeated-run variance is not provided. This makes it harder to assess the stability of small differences, especially against DINOv2 or between model variants.

The efficiency discussion is useful but incomplete. Runtime is reported per single-image classification on one A100, but class-count scaling, batching behavior, memory constraints, and total training cost are not analyzed in much depth. For 1000-class generative classification, the method remains expensive relative to standard discriminative classifiers.

The comparison to diffusion classifiers is strong for standard multi-step DiT/SiT evaluation, but the treatment of faster diffusion or consistency-style alternatives is limited. The MeanFlow appendix helps, yet it is not enough to fully settle the practical speed comparison against the broader family of modern few-step generative models.

Baseline fairness has a few caveats: some baselines are reproduced while others use public checkpoints; the MaskGIT comparison uses an unofficial checkpoint; generalization beyond RandAR is shown only at smaller scale; and the DINOv2 comparison is limited to linear probing rather than broader discriminative adaptation protocols.

The robustness story is promising but somewhat overstated. ImageNet-C is represented by only Gaussian noise and JPEG at one severity, and WILDS results vary by dataset/model size, with DiT matching or slightly exceeding RandAR on some FMoW metrics. The conclusions should be framed as strong evidence rather than definitive robustness superiority.

The paper would benefit from clearer discussion of limitations, especially dependence on class-conditional generative pretraining, sensitivity to tokenizer design, computational cost for many classes, and whether order marginalization still helps under larger-scale pretraining or non-object-centric recognition tasks.
